cues.text: A Boy Drawn to the Desert
Born Youssef Antoun Makhlouf in 1828 in the mountain village of Bekaa Kafra in northern Lebanon, Sharbel lost his father, a mule driver, at only three years old.
As a boy tending his family's flock, he built a small grotto to the Blessed Virgin Mary, where he prayed regularly.
He grew fascinated by two uncles who lived as hermits at a nearby monastery—an early sign of a vocation that would shape his entire life.
Entering the Maronite Order

At twenty-three, Sharbel entered the Lebanese Maronite Order , taking the religious name Sharbel in honor of a second-century Antiochene martyr, and made his final vows at the Monastery of St. Maron in Annaya in 1853.
He was ordained a priest in 1859 after completing theological studies.
He then spent sixteen years in community life at the monastery, marked by intense devotion to the Eucharist and rigorous personal asceticism.
Fellow monks noted these qualities even amid the ordinary discipline of monastic life.
The Miracle of the Lamp
Tradition holds that Sharbel's superior granted his request to become a hermit only after witnessing what came to be called the 'miracle of the lamp.'
A worker had mistakenly filled Sharbel's oil lamp with water instead of oil.
Yet the lamp continued to burn steadily through the night regardless.
Twenty-Three Years in Solitude
In 1875, Sharbel entered the remote hermitage of Saints Peter and Paul, some 1,200 meters above the monastery.

He spent the final twenty-three years of his life there in near-total solitude, prayer, and extreme fasting, emerging only rarely, at his superiors' occasional request, to minister to nearby villages.
Death and Incorruption
Sharbel suffered a stroke while celebrating Mass on 16 December 1898 and died eight days later, on Christmas Eve.

Within months, monks reported seeing mysterious light around his tomb; when his body was exhumed, it was found remarkably incorrupt, reportedly still exuding blood and a mysterious oil-like substance associated with numerous reported healings.
Legacy
Beatified in 1965 at the close of the Second Vatican Council and canonized in 1977 by Pope Paul VI, Sharbel is venerated today not only by Christians.
Notably, many Muslims and Druze across Lebanon are drawn by his reputation for holiness and healing.
His deliberately hidden life became, after his death, one of the most widely known and beloved witnesses of the modern Maronite Church.
